adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old lighthouse had stood at the edge of the harbour for more than a century, and in that time it had survived storms that tore the roofs off the fishermen's cottages and floods that carried rowing boats into the high street. The keeper, a quiet man named Elias, climbed the hundred and twelve steps twice each night, once at dusk and once before dawn, to trim the wick and polish the great lens. Visitors sometimes asked why he had refused the automatic lamp the council offered him, and he would shrug and say that a machine could not tell the difference between fog and clear weather, could not hear the bell of a boat in trouble, and could not remember the names of the men who had drowned in the shallows during the winter of the great gale. He kept a ledger in the watch room, and into it he copied the weather, the shipping, and the small events of the town: a christening, a quarrel over a boundary wall, the arrival of a stranger who asked too many questions and left before the morning ferry returned. The children of the village believed the lighthouse was haunted, and Elias never corrected them, because the rumour kept them from climbing the stairs and falling through the rotten boards. In the spring a young woman arrived from the mainland with a camera and a notebook, explaining that she was writing a history of the coast and that she had a particular interest in the men who had kept the light. Elias let her sit in the watch room while he worked, and answered her questions about the storms, the ships and the long winters, though he would not say what he had written on the last page of the ledger. By midsummer she had filled three notebooks and had begun to photograph the ledger page by page, and the two of them fell into a routine of tea at four and stories until the light failed. When her book appeared two years later the dedication named no one, but the first chapter described a keeper who climbed a hundred and twelve steps in the dark and never once complained, and the village, which had always suspected the stranger of prying, decided that it had been wrong.
